explainer.subject: Chemistry
explainer.title: Aniline vs Aliphatic Amines: Basicity

steps.say: It might seem that the large benzene ring in aniline would push more electron density toward the nitrogen, making aniline a stronger base than methylamine.
Basicity depends on how easily the nitrogen's lone pair can be donated to a proton ($H^+$). If the lone pair is busy elsewhere, basicity drops.
In aniline, the lone pair on nitrogen is in conjugation with the pi-electrons of the benzene ring, spreading out over the whole molecule via resonance.
Accepting a proton would 'lock' the lone pair, destroying the resonance stability of the ring-nitrogen system. Aniline is much more stable as it is.
Aliphatic amines are more basic than ammonia, and ammonia is significantly more basic than aniline due to this delocalisation.
In methylamine, the $CH_3$ group actually pushes electrons ($+I$ effect) toward nitrogen, keeping the lone pair localized and ready to react.
Always check: is the nitrogen lone pair 'free' or 'busy' in resonance? If it's part of a ring's resonance, the amine is a weak base.

explainer.takeaway: Aniline is a weaker base because its lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring by resonance.
